questions.q: How is Immunization defined in the uploaded presentation?
options: A) The process of inducing immunity by stimulating the immune system through antigens to protect against disease
B) The passive transfer of maternal T-lymphocytes during the third trimester
C) The surgical removal of lymphoid tissue to prevent autoimmune reactivity
D) The administration of broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics prior to viral exposure
questions.hint: Inducing immunity by introducing antigens to stimulate the immune system against disease.
questions.explanation: Immunization is defined as the process of inducing immunity by introducing antigens to stimulate an active immune response, serving as a cost-effective public health tool that averts an estimated 4.4 million deaths annually.

questions.q: Global coverage of the third dose of DTP (DTP3) vaccine is frequently used as a benchmark for what public health metric?
options: A) The global prevalence of congenital primary immunodeficiencies
B) The rate of hospital-acquired surgical site infections
C) How well countries are providing routine childhood immunization services
D) The effectiveness of vector control programs against malaria
questions.hint: DTP3 coverage reflects how well routine childhood immunization services are delivered.
questions.explanation: DTP3 coverage is used worldwide as a key indicator marker for assessing how effectively national routine immunization services reach pediatric populations.

questions.q: Which type of vaccine utilizes a weakened form of the wild pathogen to generate an immune response?
options: A) Inactivated vaccine
B) Live-attenuated vaccine
C) Toxoid vaccine
D) Subunit/Conjugate vaccine
questions.hint: A live-attenuated vaccine uses a weakened form of the living pathogen.
questions.explanation: Live-attenuated vaccines incorporate a weakened form of the living germ that replicates harmlessly to trigger robust humoral and cellular memory without causing severe disease in healthy hosts.

questions.q: What type of vaccine is formulated using a harmful protein product produced by a bacterium rather than the bacterium itself?
options: A) mRNA vaccine
B) Viral vector vaccine
C) Inactivated vaccine
D) Toxoid vaccine
questions.hint: Toxoid vaccines use inactivated bacterial toxins.
questions.explanation: Toxoid vaccines (such as tetanus or diphtheria toxoids) utilize inactivated bacterial toxins (toxoids) to elicit neutralizing antibodies against toxin-mediated pathogenesis.

questions.q: In what year was the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) originally launched globally by the WHO?
questions.hint: WHO launched EPI globally in 1974.
questions.explanation: The WHO officially launched the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) in 1974 to ensure universal access to life-saving vaccines for children in all nations.

questions.q: In Tanzania, what national name is given to the initiative established in 1975 to manage public immunization services?
options: A) The Expanded Child Survival Network (ECSN)
B) The National Vaccine Safety Bureau (NVSB)
C) The Immunization and Vaccine Development (IVD) program
D) The Pediatric Infectious Disease Prevention Agency (PIDPA)
questions.hint: Immunization and Vaccine Development (IVD) program.
questions.explanation: The national immunization initiative in Tanzania is officially named the Immunization and Vaccine Development (IVD) program, established in 1975.

questions.q: According to the national schedule, which vaccines are administered at BIRTH?
options: A) Pentavalent 1 and PCV 1
B) BCG and OPV 0 (up to 14 days)
C) Measles-Rubella 1 (MR 1) and Rotavac 1
D) IPV and HPV 1
questions.hint: BCG and OPV 0 (within 14 days).
questions.explanation: At birth, infants receive intradermal BCG (0.05 mL in the right upper arm) and oral OPV 0 (2 drops in the mouth, given within the first 14 days of life).

questions.q: At what age is the first dose of Measles-Rubella (MR 1) vaccine administered in the routine schedule?
options: A) 6 weeks
B) 14 weeks
C) 6 months
D) 9 months
questions.hint: MR 1 is given at 9 months of age.
questions.explanation: The first dose of Measles-Rubella (MR 1) is administered at 9 months of age as a 0.5 mL subcutaneous injection in the left upper arm.

questions.q: What is the single UNIVERSAL contraindication to any routine immunization procedure?
options: A) A personal history of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a vaccine component or previous dose
B) Mild upper respiratory tract infection without fever
C) A family history of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)
D) Concomitant administration of topical dermatological steroids
questions.hint: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a vaccine component or prior dose.
questions.explanation: The sole universal contraindication across all vaccines is a proven history of severe anaphylactic reaction to a prior dose or a specific component of that vaccine.

questions.q: How does the WHO define a Missed Opportunity for Vaccination (MOV)?
options: A) Refusal of a parent to allow any vaccination due to personal beliefs
B) Expiry of a vaccine vial while stored in a health facility refrigerator
C) Any contact with health services by an eligible individual that does not result in receiving overdue vaccine doses
D) Occurrence of a mild fever following routine DTP injection
questions.hint: Any health service contact by an eligible person where overdue vaccine doses are not given.
questions.explanation: An MOV occurs whenever an individual eligible for vaccination attends a healthcare facility for any reason but fails to receive the eligible vaccine doses despite having no valid contraindications.

questions.q: What is the exact anatomical site and route prescribed for administering the BCG vaccine in neonates?
options: A) Antero-lateral aspect of left thigh; Intramuscular
B) Right upper arm; Intradermal (0.05 mL)
C) Left upper arm; Subcutaneous
D) Gluteal region; Deep intramuscular
questions.hint: Right upper arm, intradermal, 0.05 mL.
questions.explanation: BCG is administered strictly via the intradermal route into the right upper arm at a precise volume of 0.05 mL.

questions.q: Which five antigens are combined within the Pentavalent vaccine formulation?
options: A) Measles, Mumps, Rubella, Varicella, and Polio
B) Bacillus Calmette-Guérin, Rotavirus, Pneumococcus, Polio, and HPV
C) Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis, Influenza, and Hepatitis A
D) Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (DPT-HepB-Hib)
questions.hint: DPT-HepB-Hib: Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B, and Hib.
questions.explanation: The Pentavalent vaccine protects against five diseases: Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B, and Hib.

questions.q: At what specific infant ages are the primary three doses of Pentavalent, PCV, and Rotavac vaccines scheduled?
options: A) 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks
B) 1 month, 2 months, and 3 months
C) 2 months, 4 months, and 6 months
D) 6 weeks, 9 months, and 18 months
questions.hint: 6, 10, and 14 weeks.
questions.explanation: Routine primary infant immunization rounds occur at 6 weeks (dose 1), 10 weeks (dose 2), and 14 weeks (dose 3).

questions.q: At week 14 of the schedule, which injectable polio vaccine dose is added alongside OPV 3, Pentavalent 3, PCV 3, and Rotavac 3?
options: A) Oral Polio Booster
B) Subcutaneous Yellow Fever
C) Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) via injection
D) Intradermal BCG booster
questions.hint: Injectable Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) is added at 14 weeks.
questions.explanation: At 14 weeks of age, one dose of injectable Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) is administered alongside OPV 3 and other 14-week vaccines.

questions.q: What is the correct dose and volume for Rotavac oral vaccine at each administration?
options: A) 2 drops
B) 5 drops (0.5 mL)
C) 10 drops (1.0 mL)
D) 1 drop
questions.hint: 5 drops (0.5 mL) orally.
questions.explanation: Rotavac is administered orally as 5 drops (0.5 mL) per dose at weeks 6, 10, and 14.

questions.q: Where are Pentavalent and PCV vaccines injected relative to each other during a 6-week immunization visit?
options: A) Both are injected into the left upper arm
B) Both are given as a single combined oral solution
C) Pentavalent into the left arm; PCV into the right arm
D) Pentavalent into the antero-lateral aspect of the left thigh; PCV into the antero-lateral aspect of the right thigh
questions.hint: Pentavalent in the left anterolateral thigh; PCV in the right anterolateral thigh.
questions.explanation: To prevent local confusion, Pentavalent (0.5 mL IM) is injected into the left anterolateral thigh, while PCV (0.5 mL IM) is injected into the right anterolateral thigh.

questions.q: What integrated Deworming regimen (Mebendazole) is prescribed for children aged 12–23 months versus children 24 months and above?
options: A) 12–23 months: 1 tablet (500 mg) single dose; 24 months+: 1 tablet (500 mg) every 6 months
B) 12–23 months: 200 mg syrup daily for 5 days; 24 months+: 1000 mg single dose
C) 12–23 months: Albendazole 400 mg; 24 months+: Mebendazole is contraindicated
D) 12–23 months: No deworming allowed; 24 months+: 1 tablet yearly
questions.hint: 500 mg once for 12–23 months; 500 mg every 6 months from 24 months onward.
questions.explanation: Integrated EPI services specify 1 tablet of Mebendazole (500 mg) once for children 12–23 months, and 1 tablet (500 mg) every 6 months for children 24 months and older.

questions.q: According to integrated Vitamin A supplementation guidelines, what dose is administered to non-breastfed infants aged 0–5 months (6th week), at 6 complete months, and to children 12–59 months?
options: A) All ages receive a uniform dose of 100,000 IU
B) 0–5 months: 10,000 IU; 6 months: 50,000 IU; 12–59 months: 100,000 IU
C) 0–5 months: 50,000 IU (once); 6 months: 100,000 IU (once); 12–59 months: 200,000 IU (every 6 months)
D) Vitamin A is administered only after 5 years of age
questions.hint: 50,000 IU at 6 weeks (non-breastfed), 100,000 IU at 6 months, and 200,000 IU every 6 months from 12–59 months.
questions.explanation: Vitamin A schedule specifies: 50,000 IU at 6 weeks for non-breastfed infants, 100,000 IU at 6 months, and 200,000 IU every 6 months for ages 12–59 months.

questions.q: What delivery strategy is utilized by the national IVD program to reach nomadic and distant hard-to-reach communities requiring overnight stays?
options: A) Fixed facility delivery
B) Mobile clinics
C) School-based health visits
D) Direct mail delivery
questions.hint: Mobile clinics reach remote or nomadic communities with overnight trips.
questions.explanation: To access remote or nomadic populations, IVD employs mobile clinics using vehicles that carry equipment and health teams for overnight field trips.

questions.q: What target group receives the HPV vaccine in the national schedule, and at what dosage/route?
options: A) Pregnant women; 1.0 mL Subcutaneous
B) Adolescent boys aged 10 years; Oral drops
C) Infants at 9 months; 0.05 mL Intradermal
D) Girls aged 9–14 years; 0.5 mL Intramuscular in the left upper arm
questions.hint: Girls aged 9–14 years; 0.5 mL IM in the left upper arm.
questions.explanation: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine is targeted at young girls (ages 9–14) as a 0.5 mL IM injection in the left upper arm.

questions.q: Which of the following conditions is an ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION to administering live-attenuated vaccines (e.g., BCG, OPV, Rotavirus, MR)?
options: A) Severe immunocompromised state (e.g., symptomatic HIV, active leukemia/lymphoma, or receiving chemotherapy/radiotherapy)
B) Presence of a mild common cold without fever
C) Current dermatological nappy rash
D) Exclusive breastfeeding
questions.hint: Severe immunocompromise (such as symptomatic HIV, leukemia/lymphoma, or chemotherapy).
questions.explanation: Live vaccines are strictly contraindicated in severely immunocompromised children because impaired cellular immunity allows uncontrolled replication of the attenuated vaccine virus.

questions.q: Which clinical scenario represents a TRUE contraindication to a second dose of the SAME vaccine?
options: A) Mild localized swelling (<2 cm) at the injection site resolving in 24 hours
B) Temperature of 37.8°C recorded 6 hours post-injection
C) Occurrence of an anaphylactic reaction, convulsion, or encephalopathy/altered consciousness within 72 hours of the previous dose
D) History of physiological jaundice during the neonatal period
questions.hint: Anaphylaxis, convulsion, or encephalopathy/altered consciousness within 72 hours of a prior dose.
questions.explanation: Severe systemic adverse events (anaphylaxis, seizures, altered GCS) within 72 hours of vaccination represent absolute contraindications to subsequent doses of that specific vaccine product.

questions.q: Which of the following conditions is FALSELY considered a contraindication and SHOULD NOT delay routine vaccination?
options: A) Active untreated pulmonary tuberculosis
B) Mild upper respiratory tract infection (common cold) without significant fever, or minor local reaction to a previous dose
C) High-dose systemic chemotherapy for acute leukemia
D) Severe acute febrile illness requiring inpatient hospitalization
questions.hint: A mild cold without significant fever or a minor prior local reaction does not delay vaccination.
questions.explanation: Mild illnesses (colds, mild diarrhea without fever), previous minor local redness, breastfeeding, and completed antibiotic courses are false contraindications; vaccination should proceed normally.

questions.q: Why are chronic chest diseases (e.g., Cystic Fibrosis) and Congenital Heart Disease considered IMPORTANT INDICATIONS rather than contraindications for immunization?
options: A) They accelerate vaccine metabolism in the liver
B) Vaccines cure the underlying structural heart defect
C) These children have no active B-lymphocytes
D) These underlying conditions place children at significantly higher risk for severe morbidity and mortality from vaccine-preventable respiratory infections
questions.hint: They increase risk of severe complications from vaccine-preventable infections.
questions.explanation: Children with chronic cardiac or pulmonary compromise suffer disproportionately severe complications if infected with pathogens like measles, pertussis, or pneumococcus, making timely vaccination vital.

questions.q: How is an Adverse Event Following Immunization (AEFI) defined in public health monitoring?
options: A) Any untoward medical occurrence following immunization that does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the usage of the vaccine
B) A proven toxic manufacturing error present in every batch of a vaccine
C) A legal claim filed by a patient against a healthcare worker
D) An immediate allergic skin reaction occurring exclusively within 60 seconds of injection
questions.hint: Any untoward medical event after immunization, regardless of proven causality.
questions.explanation: An AEFI is any untoward medical event occurring after vaccination, regardless of whether a direct causal connection to the vaccine product exists.

questions.q: What three reporting categories are used to classify AEFIs based on clinical severity?
options: A) Transient, Permanent, and Terminal
B) Immediate, Delayed, and Late-onset
C) Minor, Severe, and Serious
D) Local, Regional, and Systemic
questions.hint: Minor, severe, and serious.
questions.explanation: For public health reporting, AEFIs are categorized into Minor, Severe, and Serious reactions.

questions.q: What features characterize MINOR vaccine reactions?
options: A) High risk of permanent paralysis and brain damage
B) Common, self-limiting reactions occurring within a few hours (e.g., pain, mild swelling, redness at injection site, low-grade fever, irritability) that pose little danger
C) Mandatory requirement for inpatient ICU admission
D) Occurrence exclusively after 6 months from vaccination
questions.hint: Common, mild, self-limiting reactions like soreness, minor swelling, or low fever.
questions.explanation: Minor AEFI reactions are brief, localized or mild systemic responses (injection site soreness, low fever) triggered by normal immune activation.

questions.q: What criteria classify an AEFI as a SERIOUS Adverse Event?
options: A) Minor local itching lasting 10 minutes
B) Mild fever of 38.1°C that responds to paracetamol
C) Temporary fussiness lasting 1 hour
D) Event resulting in death, inpatient hospitalization, persistent/significant disability, an AEFI cluster, or evoking significant community concern
questions.hint: Death, hospitalization, persistent disability, cluster event, or major community concern.
questions.explanation: A serious AEFI meets severe outcome thresholds: fatality, hospitalization, permanent disability, congenital anomaly, or cluster events causing public panic.

questions.q: Which of the five WHO cause-specific categories describes an AEFI caused by an inherent property of the vaccine product itself?
options: A) Vaccine product-related reaction
B) Vaccine quality defect-related reaction
C) Immunization error-related reaction
D) Coincidental event
questions.hint: Due to an inherent property of the vaccine product itself.
questions.explanation: A vaccine product-related reaction stems directly from an inherent pharmacological/immunological property of the properly manufactured vaccine (e.g., extensive arm swelling following DTP).

questions.q: An outbreak of staphylococcal abscesses occurring at a health facility due to the reuse of a single contaminated multi-dose vaccine vial is classified under which AEFI category?
options: A) Vaccine product-related reaction
B) Immunization anxiety-related reaction
C) Immunization error-related reaction
D) Coincidental event
questions.hint: Contamination or improper handling/technique is an immunization error-related reaction.
questions.explanation: Infections or injuries caused by improper handling, reconstitution, storage, or administration technique (e.g., contaminated vials) are immunization error-related reactions.

questions.q: A case of paralytic poliomyelitis occurring because a manufacturer failed to completely inactivate a lot of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) represents which AEFI cause category?
options: A) Vaccine product-related reaction
B) Vaccine quality defect-related reaction
C) Immunization anxiety-related reaction
D) Coincidental event
questions.hint: A manufacturing/inactivation flaw is a vaccine quality defect-related reaction.
questions.explanation: Flaws arising from manufacturing errors, inadequate inactivation, or device failure fall under vaccine quality defect-related reactions.

questions.q: An adolescent girl experiences vasovagal syncope (fainting) immediately following HPV vaccination due to fear of the needle. How is this AEFI classified?
options: A) Vaccine product-related reaction
B) Vaccine quality defect-related reaction
C) Coincidental event
D) Immunization anxiety-related reaction
questions.hint: Fainting from needle fear is an immunization anxiety-related reaction.
questions.explanation: Vasovagal syncope, hyperventilation, or panic-induced symptoms surrounding the injection process represent immunization anxiety-related reactions.

questions.q: An infant develops a high fever and is diagnosed with acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria 4 hours after receiving routine 10-week vaccinations. What type of AEFI is this?
options: A) Coincidental event
B) Vaccine product-related reaction
C) Immunization error-related reaction
D) Vaccine quality defect
questions.hint: An unrelated illness occurring by chance around vaccination time is a coincidental event.
questions.explanation: A coincidental AEFI occurs when an underlying illness (such as malaria) manifests at the time of vaccination purely by temporal association, unrelated to the vaccine.

questions.q: How is an 'AEFI Cluster' defined in epidemiology?
options: A) A single patient experiencing 5 different side effects simultaneously
B) A national increase in vaccine costs over 5 years
C) Two or more cases of the same adverse event related in time, place, or vaccine administered
D) The routine co-administration of Pentavalent and PCV vaccines
questions.hint: Two or more cases of the same adverse event linked by time, place, or vaccine.
questions.explanation: An AEFI cluster involves 2 or more similar adverse events grouped by location, time frame, specific healthcare provider, or shared vaccine lot/vial.

questions.q: What operational mechanism is defined as 'Catch-Up Vaccination'?
options: A) Administering double doses of vaccines to accelerate growth
B) Vaccinating an individual who is overdue or missing routine vaccine doses for which they are eligible per the national schedule
C) Vaccinating elderly grandparents alongside infants
D) Substituting oral vaccines for injectable vaccines during epidemics
questions.hint: Giving overdue or missed routine vaccine doses to eligible individuals.
questions.explanation: Catch-up vaccination strategies focus on identifying and immunizing individuals who missed scheduled doses, restoring population coverage.

questions.q: According to the WHO MOV strategy, what four-step framework guides health facilities to eliminate missed opportunities?
options: A) Pre-screen, Quarantine, Inject, Report
B) Isolate, Sanitize, Vaccinate, Discharge
C) Audit, Fine, Suspend, Retrain
D) Assessment, Analysis, Action, and Impact
questions.hint: Assessment, Analysis, Action, and Impact.
questions.explanation: The WHO MOV strategy uses a four-phase methodology: Assessment (quantifying MOVs), Analysis (identifying root causes), Action (revising workflows), and Impact (measuring coverage improvement).

questions.q: What operational strategy can health facilities use to monitor monthly immunization coverage and detect drop-outs?
options: A) Standard monthly monitoring charts tracking coverage and doses administered
B) Annual door-to-door census surveys only
C) Measuring infant weight every 2 weeks
D) Testing serum IgG levels in every child at every visit
questions.hint: Monthly monitoring charts tracking doses and coverage.
questions.explanation: Microplanning and routine monitoring rely on visual monthly tracking charts displayed in facilities to monitor coverage targets and drop-out rates.

questions.q: What is the recommended schedule for Tetanus-diphtheria (Td) vaccination in women of childbearing age (15–49 years)?
options: A) Single dose at age 15 only
B) Annual injections for 20 years
C) 5-dose sequence: Td-1 at first contact, Td-2 at 1 month, Td-3 at 6 months, Td-4 at 1 year, and Td-5 at 1 year after Td-4
D) Td is given only during active labor
questions.hint: 5 doses: Td-1 at first contact, Td-2 at +1 mo, Td-3 at +6 mos, Td-4 at +1 yr, Td-5 at +1 yr.
questions.explanation: The Td schedule for women of reproductive age consists of 5 doses (Td-1 at 1st visit, Td-2 +1mo, Td-3 +6mo, Td-4 +1yr, Td-5 +1yr) to establish lifelong protection against maternal and neonatal tetanus.

questions.q: Which of the following describes an AEFI cluster caused by improper cold chain management?
options: A) Anaphylaxis in a single child with egg allergy
B) Multiple infants developing severe local sterile abscesses or loss of potency after receiving vaccines that were accidentally frozen during transport
C) A child developing a runny nose 3 weeks after OPV
D) Fainting in 10 adults receiving yellow fever vaccine
questions.hint: Freezing freeze-sensitive vaccines can cause sterile abscesses or loss of potency.
questions.explanation: Freezing aluminum-adjuvanted vaccines alters physical stability, predisposing to localized sterile abscess clusters or treatment failure.

questions.q: Is an infant who recently completed a course of oral antibiotics for a mild skin infection eligible for routine 6-week vaccinations?
options: A) No, antibiotics neutralize all live and inactivated vaccines
B) No, vaccination must be delayed for 6 months after antibiotics
C) Yes, but only if given via the intradermal route
D) Yes, a recently completed antibiotic course is NOT a contraindication
questions.hint: Recent or completed antibiotic therapy does not contraindicate routine vaccines.
questions.explanation: Antibiotic usage does not interfere with the antibody response to routine pediatric vaccines and is not a reason to withhold immunization.

questions.q: A mother brings her 10-week-old infant to the clinic for a routine weight check. The health worker notes that the child received BCG and OPV 0 at birth, but missed the 6-week vaccines. The child has no fever or acute illness. What is the correct clinical action?
options: A) Administer OPV 1, Pentavalent 1, PCV 1, and Rotavac 1 immediately at this visit (avoiding a Missed Opportunity for Vaccination)
B) Turn the mother away and tell her to return exactly when the child is 6 months old
C) Restart the entire vaccination schedule from birth by re-injecting BCG
D) Administer only oral Vitamin A and withhold all vaccines
questions.hint: Give the missed 6-week vaccines right away without restarting the schedule.
questions.explanation: Under catch-up guidelines and MOV elimination protocols, any eligible child attending a facility should receive overdue doses immediately without restarting the series or turning them away.

questions.q: A 14-week-old infant receives OPV 3, Pentavalent 3, PCV 3, Rotavac 3, and IPV 1. Six hours later, the infant develops a temperature of 38.2°C, mild fussiness, and redness (1 cm) at the thigh injection site. How is this AEFI classified by severity, what is the cause category, and what is the appropriate management?
options: A) Serious AEFI; Immunization error; Hospitalize in ICU immediately
B) Severe AEFI; Quality defect; Administer high-dose IV corticosteroids
C) Minor AEFI; Vaccine product-related reaction; Reassure the mother, advise supportive care/paracetamol, and emphasize that this is a normal self-limiting immune response
D) Coincidental AEFI; Anxiety-related; Permanent contraindication to future vaccines
questions.hint: Low fever and minor local redness = minor vaccine product-related reaction; reassure and give supportive care.
questions.explanation: Low fever and minor local inflammation within hours of DPT/Pentavalent vaccination represent a typical minor vaccine product-related reaction requiring symptomatic care and parental reassurance.

questions.q: A 12-month-old child with known acute lymphoblastic leukemia currently receiving high-dose systemic chemotherapy presents to the clinic. The mother requests the 9-month Measles-Rubella (MR 1) vaccine, which was missed earlier. What is the correct management decision?
options: A) Administer MR 1 immediately because measles is dangerous
B) Contraindicate MR 1 at this time because live-attenuated vaccines (MR) are strictly contraindicated during severe immunosuppressive chemotherapy
C) Administer a double dose of MR 1 subcutaneously
D) Substitute MR 1 with oral polio vaccine
questions.hint: Live vaccines like MR are contraindicated during active immunosuppressive chemotherapy.
questions.explanation: Active malignancy and immunosuppressive chemotherapy are absolute contraindications to live vaccines (MR, BCG, OPV) due to the risk of severe vaccine-derived disease; live vaccines are deferred until immune recovery.

questions.q: Why are Albendazole tablets NOT recommended for deworming in infants aged 12–23 months under the integrated EPI schedule?
options: A) Albendazole neutralizes Measles-Rubella antibodies
B) Albendazole causes severe hyperkalemia in infants
C) Mebendazole is the preferred first-line agent for 12–23 months; Albendazole (400 mg) is approved as second-line therapy only for children 24 months and older
D) Albendazole is an injectable vaccine
questions.hint: Mebendazole is used for 12–23 months; albendazole (400 mg) is second-line for ≥24 months.
questions.explanation: Integrated service protocols specify Mebendazole (500 mg) for ages 12–23 months, reserving Albendazole (400 mg) as second-line deworming for age 24 months and above.

questions.q: A health facility reports 5 cases of deep tissue abscesses at the left thigh injection site among different infants who all received Pentavalent 1 on the same morning from the same healthcare worker. What epidemiological entity is this, what is the likely cause category, and what immediate action is needed?
options: A) AEFI Cluster; Immunization error-related reaction (unsterile technique or contaminated multidose vial); Halt use of the specific open vial, investigate operational practices, and audit cold chain/injection safety
B) Coincidental cluster; Vaccine product-related; No action needed
C) Minor AEFI; Anxiety-related; Ban all pentavalent vaccinations nationally
D) Normal expected reaction; Quality defect; Discharge patients without care
questions.hint: Multiple similar local abscesses from one session = AEFI cluster due to immunization error; stop the vial and investigate.
questions.explanation: Multiple identical local bacterial infections arising from a single clinic session define an AEFI cluster caused by programmatic/administration errors (contamination), requiring immediate field investigation and practice audit.

questions.q: How does the WHO define 'Zero-Dose Children' in global immunization tracking?
options: A) Children who have received all routine vaccines but no booster shots
B) Children who experience zero side effects after vaccination
C) Children who have not received any routine vaccines (specifically measured as lacking the first dose of DTP/Pentavalent)
D) Infants born with zero detectable serum antibodies
questions.hint: Children missing routine vaccines, tracked by lacking DTP1/Pentavalent 1.
questions.explanation: 'Zero-dose children' is an epidemiological term referring to children who have received no routine vaccinations, operationally measured by failure to receive DTP1/Pentavalent 1.

questions.q: Which of the following children SHOULD receive routine vaccinations today without delay?
options: A) A child with an active anaphylactic reaction to egg protein receiving flu vaccine
B) A child with a mild runny nose, temperature of 37.1°C, who is alert, playing, and eating well
C) A child in septic shock with a GCS of 6 in the ICU
D) A child with active untreated fulminant tuberculosis
questions.hint: An alert, well child with a mild runny nose and normal temperature has no valid contraindication.
questions.explanation: Minor afebrile upper respiratory symptoms are false contraindications; withholding vaccines in this setting creates unnecessary missed opportunities.

questions.q: When administering Td vaccine to a 25-year-old pregnant woman attending her first antenatal visit (with no prior documented tetanus vaccination history), what is the correct schedule?
options: A) Give 1 dose at delivery
B) Give Td-1 today, Td-2 after 5 years
C) Td is contraindicated in pregnancy
D) Administer Td-1 today at first contact, Td-2 one month later (at least 2 weeks before delivery), and Td-3 six months later
questions.hint: Td-1 at first contact, Td-2 one month later, and Td-3 six months later.
questions.explanation: Maternal tetanus protection requires Td-1 at first ANC contact, Td-2 1 month later (providing acute protection for delivery), followed by Td-3 at 6 months to build long-term immunity.

questions.q: What is the rationale behind administering Hepatitis B vaccine as part of the Pentavalent formulation at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age?
options: A) To establish early active immunity against chronic Hepatitis B virus infection and prevent childhood cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
B) To treat acute hepatitis A gastroenteritis
C) To replace the need for BCG vaccination
D) To prevent acute rotavirus diarrhea
questions.hint: Prevents chronic Hepatitis B infection and long-term liver cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.explanation: Infant Hepatitis B vaccination induces early protective antibody levels, preventing chronic carrier states, liver cirrhosis, and long-term risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.q: In evaluating an AEFI case, how is a 'Vaccine Quality Defect-Related Reaction' distinguished from an 'Immunization Error-Related Reaction'?
options: A) Quality defects affect only adult vaccines; errors affect only infant vaccines
B) Quality defects cause fever; errors cause pain
C) Quality defects arise from manufacturing or device flaws provided by the producer; errors arise from improper handling, storage, or administration by healthcare staff
D) Quality defects are always coincidental; errors are always product-related
questions.hint: Quality defect = manufacturer/device flaw; immunization error = improper handling, storage, or administration.
questions.explanation: Quality defects reflect flaws originating from the manufacturer (e.g., inadequate inactivation), whereas immunization errors result from human operational failures in cold chain maintenance, preparation, or injection technique.
